summary:
Mali's new penal code, announced in October 2024 and in force from 13 December 2024, criminalises same-sex conduct, which had not previously been a criminal offence, and carries harsh penalties. The statute also bans the undefined offence of "promoting" homosexuality and reaches any citizen seen to encourage it, which widens the range of people who can be prosecuted beyond those accused of conduct itself.

Human Rights Watch reported on 6 November 2024 that the drafting is broad enough for expansive application. Even before the new code, vague "public indecency" provisions in Article 225 were used against LGBT people and gender-nonconforming expression, so presentation rather than conduct has historically been the basis for police attention.

The change came under the military junta, which has at the same time clamped down on opposition and media. Human Rights Watch's 2025 world report on Mali covers junta rule, counterterrorism sweeps that included the arbitrary arrest of 25 people in Ouro Fero village in the Nara region, and an ICC arrest warrant. That chapter contains no trans-specific content and no information on how trans prisoners are housed, held in special units, or segregated. Independent judicial recourse and civil-society channels are correspondingly constrained.

Instability from armed groups forms part of the environment a visitor enters: the US State Department's 2021 human rights report on Mali recorded violence and instability from armed groups alongside significant societal stigma toward LGBT people, at a time when same-sex conduct was still not criminalised.
tangentialFactors:
The legal position shifted within three years. The US State Department's 2021 report assessed that same-sex conduct was not criminalised in Mali while documenting significant societal stigma; the 2024 code removes that distinction between lawful status and social exposure. Its 2011 report had already listed discrimination based on sexual orientation among the country's human-rights problems, alongside gender inequality, FGM and corruption, indicating a long-standing pattern of stigma that predates criminalisation.

Criminalisation was adopted in the same period as wider restrictions on political opposition and media under the junta, so the new offence sits inside a general contraction of dissent rather than as an isolated statutory change.

Counterterrorism operations continue to produce arbitrary detention. The arrest of 25 people in Ouro Fero village in the Nara region, documented by Human Rights Watch for 2024, illustrates the sweep-and-detain pattern a visitor may encounter in areas of active operations, alongside armed-group violence recorded by the State Department.
localsOnly:
The new code applies to Malian citizens as well as to foreign nationals, and its language covering anyone seen to encourage homosexuality exposes residents, including those who merely associate with or speak for LGBT people, to prosecution. Human Rights Watch notes that the undefined "promotion" offence greatly expands who can be charged.

Residents lived with the practical effects of Article 225 before the code took effect: the public indecency provisions were used against LGBT people and against gender-nonconforming expression, so gender-nonconforming Malians have faced police action on the basis of appearance. Societal stigma was documented by the US State Department in 2011 and again in 2021.

Under the junta, clampdowns on opposition and media limit the channels through which residents can challenge charges or seek protection, and counterterrorism sweeps have produced arbitrary arrests such as the detention of 25 people in Ouro Fero village in the Nara region.
outOfScopeNotes:
The Human Dignity Trust country profile for Mali was not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403), so its documentation of the new criminalisation is not independently reproduced here and remains unverified from that source.

The Human Rights Watch World Report 2025 Mali chapter contains no trans-specific content and no finding on prison placement, special units, or segregation for trans detainees; how trans prisoners are held in Mali is unresolved and not sourced.

The inventory does not specify the penalties attached to the new offences beyond the description "harsh penalties", and does not address entry or visa screening that could disclose a person's status, identity-document or gender-marker rules, restroom and facilities access, hate-crime protection, marriage or partner recognition, or access to gender-affirming care in Mali. These are not sourced either way.

The US State Department's 2021 report predates the 2024 penal code and describes the earlier legal position; its assessment of non-criminalisation no longer reflects the law in force since 13 December 2024.
